comments.author: aloys
comments.text:
This is the most grounded take I have seen on AI-assisted coding so far.

I love how Mitchell shows that:


There is friction in learning to use AI-coding tools, it's not all magic. First and foremost, it's a tool.

The productivity gains don't seem overinflated, it's a nice addition to his flow (for PR triage for example) - but he treats it like a tool, nothing else.

It's only useful because he's a talented dev. to start with, with a proven, deep expertise.

He's not pushing for, or against AI.

He is genuinely concerned about junior devs, who might be tempted to skip the fundamentals. This worries me too. It reminds me of the some React devs with no idea of (or interest in) the underlying web technologies; but across the entire CS board.


If someone like Mitchell gets a limited boost of productivity, it shows that a lot of people out there over estimate AI gains (by lack of expertise, experience, or bias).

By "limited" I'm not saying there isn't a net gain (he says he reached the point of "no way I can go back") but more that it is not the panacea that we are led to believe. He uses to automate what's worth automating.

I also note how he uses it as an enhancement to his skillset, not a replacement; he provides scripts, testing. He seems very much in control of the actual engineering.

Mitchell is not your average developer, he's definitively on the far right hand side of the bell curve of software engineering skills.
And Mitchell still codes by hand; I'm glad to see this as a counter argument that "coding is over".

Highly worth a read, for both pro / anti AI ( and those like me sitting on the fence).

Some great quotes:


I interrupt the agent, not the other way around



I felt more efficient, but even if I wasn't, the thing I liked the most was that I could now focus my coding and thinking on tasks I really loved while still adequately completing the tasks I didn't.



I'd say right now I'm maybe effective at having a background agent running 10 to 20% of a normal working day.



I have no skin in the game here, and there are of course other reasons behind utility to avoid using AI. I fully respect anyone's individual decisions regarding it.



I really don't care one way or the other if AI is here to stay(3), I'm a software craftsman that just wants to build stuff for the love of the game.



(3) The skill formation issues particularly in juniors without a strong grasp of fundamentals deeply worries me, however.


edit: many typos :)

comments.author: edk-
comments.text: I really can't see the difference between this and any other pro-AI post. It mentions one downside in a footnote, but along with every other “balanced” take I've seen it notes that people have moral objections and then ignores them. It has to or there'd be nothing else to talk about. But that also means it is implicitly pro-AI, in the same way that a post about the pros and cons of arson would be necessarily pro-arson, no matter how much lip service it paid to the opposition, by having a “pros” section at all.

comments.author: mitchellh
comments.text: I didn't mean balanced in terms of pro vs anti-AI. It is very obviously pro-AI since I ended up happy with the results. I meant balanced in terms of AI capabilities compared to the dramatic, hype posts that say stuff like [obviously paraphrasing]: "AI is so amazing I wrote a compiler in 2 weeks."

comments.author: edk-
comments.text: Yeah, I think your title and introduction are descriptive and I don't feel misled by them or anything. (And I wouldn't generally comment on a post about AI just to remind everyone that anti-AI people exist). I'm just not sure why @aloys says it is “not pushing for, or against AI” when it is (openly) predicated on AI being a good thing to use. I have always been worried that the moral argument would be forgotten rather than resolved; and that's what that looks like, holding cautiously positive, technically competent takes up as not leaning one way or the other.

comments.author: aloys
comments.text:
I think I see your point @edk. Let me try to clarify what my thoughts are regarding this piece.

Talking about AI is difficult because there are so many facets to it (political, environmental, technical, ethical, philosophical...) which tends to make it a polarising subject.
There is a spectrum of opinions between "anti" and "pro", for each of those facets.
Sometimes, you feel so strongly about one of those facet that you won't evaluate the other facets.

If the ethical aspect of mass copyright infringement is insufferable for a person, that person might decide that the price is not worth paying no matter what the benefits are.

The way I interpret this article, Mitchell only wants to discuss the technical aspect.
He acknowledges the moral argument but decide not go in it; whatever are his reasons (more on this at the end).

I enjoyed the fact that the article is not hyped, and feels grounded on the "technical" aspect of AI-assisted coding.
He essentially says: "here's what I have tried and what I'm doing now [from a technical point of view]. But you do you.".

He clearly states that he doesn't care whether AI stays or not, he's not invested in it, and respects any opinions on using it, or not using it.

That's where I think that the article is refreshing. The gains of using it aren't presented as a game-changer. It's a suitable workflow for him, he prefers using it, rather than not, but he doesn't appear to push that hard for it.
In that sense, while it's explicitly "pro-AI", it also implicitly tells us that it's fine to not use it.

Also, while he is well known in his sphere, we shouldn't forget that he might be writing primarily for himself.

FWIW, I am so torn around the subject of AI that I'm always interested in reading opinions. This one was one of the most grounded and genuine I have seen when it comes to AI-assisted coding.

It made me re-evaluate my current use of the technology.

I will also avoid debating the other aspect of AI. Some of those are completely against my values and yet I'm still using it. It's a difficult personal journey as it shines a light on your identity and what you true values are.
Which is a difficult subject to write openly about.
E.g. if you tell me the technology is built on mass theft of intellectual property, I can only agree. Yet I'm still using it, so it's uncomfortable to talk about it as it questions my values.

It takes a fair bit of introspection and time to decide where you stand, what is acceptable and what is not. I can empathise with someone not wanting to debate those publicly.
It doesn't necessarily mean they accept it, they might still be battling within themselves.

Humans emotions are complex, AI is certainly testing those!

Hope this clears up my position!

Edit: typos! + clarify the implicit position "against" AI

comments.author: abnercoimbre
comments.text:
To quote an equally talented friend, who read Mitchell's article and liked it (they've done UI Tools Engineering at Bungie, creators of Halo.) Emphasis mine:


Having played a ton of factory/automation games I have a keen awareness of how effective something can be when it doesn't take any input from you and can run in the background while you work or sleep or whatever. That being said I wonder how many hours I would have to spend to get something set up that I find useful. And I wonder if things will change out from under me the minute I find a useful setup (pricing changes, new models working different, etc.)


Indeed, another commenter recently explained how they were burned:


[...] Then a new release comes up. An arbitrary fraction of your hard earned intuition is not only useless but actively harmful to getting good results with the new models. Worse you will never know which part it is without unlearning everything you learned and starting over again.
I've had to learn the quirks of three generations of frontier families now. It's not worth the hassle.


I'm torn on this. I'm friends with a game studio founder (John) following Mitchell's playbook exactly, and it seems to be working for him. But just like Mitchell, he's still relatively early in this whole process.

Credit where credit is due, Mitchell and John are attempting this with the mindset of craftsmen. I’ll dip my own toes in it as stable patterns emerge from them. I’m already overwhelmed attempting novel work without AI. Harness engineering is far too novel as well. Let others try that one for me.

comments.author: osa1
comments.text:
I thought it's a questionable idea at best. It's possible that the most effective use of AI coding is not making it write code that you'd write, but let it do it the way they work the best. Similar to collaborating with an actual human, no two people write the same exact code for the same task. If you work with a person long enough sometimes you can even tell their code from others. I don't know why an AI tool would or should be different in this regard.

It may be an interesting exercise at something, but not sure if at anything useful.

comments.author: hwayne
comments.text: It is pretty useful IME. The goal isn't to get the AI to write the exact same code as you, it's to understand the differences in how an AI would solve it to better know when you can rely on it.
